where: the "Approve and add" / "Not ours" pair at the foot of all five cards (x=272–546, y=390, 781, 1040, 1411, 1823)
finding: The reviewer's guard is on the wrong action. "Not ours" — which only takes children off Tally's own roster and drops a phone number — arms a two-step confirm with an explanatory line before it does anything. "Approve and add" — which writes into Planning Center, where there is no undo — fires on the first click, with nothing anywhere on the card saying what it writes, where, or that it cannot be taken back. A core-team member on their fourth card, moving fast because four of the five are routine, has no moment where the screen tells them the press is final. The one sentence in the whole page that names the destination is the subhead, and by the time they are deciding Dov or Beatriz it is 1300–1750px off the top of the window.
evidence: "Approve and add" is the brand-blue primary, leftmost, 167×36px, one click, no confirm state — compare ReviewPage's `confirmingDiscard` gate on the secondary. Searching the rendered text of review--desktop for "undo", "permanent", "cannot", "irreversible" returns zero hits. "Planning Center" appears exactly once in the whole page, buried in Dov Halevy's red error banner at y=1189. "nothing has gone into the church's database yet" sits at y=64 and describes the state before the press, not the consequence of it; the page is 1931px tall so it is off-screen for cards 3, 4 and 5.
direction: Put the guard where the consequence is. The brief's "undo is never a dialog" rule is scoped to the roster check mark and does not reach this screen, so a confirm step — or a short undo window on the toast, which is closer to the app's grain — is available here. At minimum the approve control should carry the destination and the finality in its own label or in a line directly beneath it, on every card, so it is legible without scrolling back to the subhead.

where: the amber merge line inside Ethan Nguyen's row (x=285–593, y=287–299) and Elena Salgado's row (x=285–583, y=1784–1796)
finding: The merge — the judgement this screen exists to make — does not read as something you can press, and the fact that would settle it is hidden behind pressing it. "2 students with this name are already on the roster" is bare 12px amber text with no background, no border, no underline at rest and no icon. On the same cards, purely informational banners use the identical colour token at the identical size with *more* chrome. So the reviewer learns, from Beatriz's card, that amber-12px-with-a-panel is a statement to read; then meets amber-12px-with-nothing and reads it as a weaker statement of the same kind. They note "there's a name clash", press the bright blue button beside it, and a duplicate Ethan Nguyen goes into Planning Center permanently.
evidence: Markup is `<button class="text-xs text-warn-400 hover:underline">`; Tailwind preflight zeroes padding and border, so the whole control is a 16px-tall line of text. Beatriz's "This registration is about to be cleared" is the same `text-xs text-warn-400` but on `bg-warn-500/10` with `ring-1 ring-warn-500/30`, full-width at y=1560. The consequential control is styled lighter than the passive notice. The two roster Ethans that would resolve it are never shown — and there is room: child rows are 1120px wide (x=272–1392) and Ade Okonjo's ink stops at x=411, leaving 981px empty; Noa Halevy's row has a 915px void between the name (ends x=412) and the "Added" badge (x=1327–1380).
direction: On a pointer viewport the candidate roster rows should not be behind a click at all — they are the comparison, and there are 900+ px of dead row per child to put them in. Showing the two candidate names with their grades inline, beside the child, both removes the click and makes the merge unmistakably an action rather than a caption. Whatever remains as a control needs button chrome that separates it from the warn banners it currently mimics.

where: the whole card stack, y=88 to 1876, against a 900px fold
finding: The reviewer arrives asking "how many of these need me to think, and how long will this take?" and the screen answers neither without a full scroll. Two of five families are decidable above the fold; the heading carries no count; and the signal that separates "needs a judgement" from "needs a yes" takes five different forms at five different depths inside the cards, so the only way to build a plan is to read the interior of all five. On a laptop that is 1031px of scrolling before the reviewer knows whether this is a two-minute Tuesday or a twenty-minute one.
evidence: Page 1931px in a 900px viewport. Approve buttons at y=390, 781, 1040, 1411, 1823 — cards 1 and 2 complete above the fold, card 3 onward not. "Families to review" (y=32) has no number beside it. The judgement signals: a 12px inline amber link 200px into card 1; nothing at all in card 2; a two-line prose paragraph in card 3; a red banner at the top of card 4; an amber banner plus a "Merged" badge plus an inline link in card 5. Externally every card is identical — same 1152px width, same ink-900 fill, same two-button foot. Each card holds roughly 400px of actual fact in a 1152px column.
direction: Two columns of cards would put all five families inside roughly one fold at this width, which is the density the screen is currently paying 1152px for and not spending. Alongside that, give the card a state readable from its outside edge — needs a decision vs needs a yes — and put the queue count in the heading so the size of the job is answered before the first scroll.

where: Beatriz Salgado, card 5, top edge y≈1476, and its amber banner at y=1560
finding: The one registration where doing nothing is itself an irreversible act is the last thing on the page, and its deadline is a phrase rather than a number. The queue is ordered newest-first, so the 26-day-old family — four days from the sweep that deletes (555) 019-3318, the only phone number Tally holds for them — sits 923px below the fold behind four families that can wait. A reviewer who gets interrupted after two cards has spent their attention on the 40-minute-old and the 2-hour-old ones. And a reviewer who does reach it is told "This registration is about to be cleared" with no date and no day count, so they cannot tell whether that means four days or four hours, and cannot decide whether it is worth phoning the number before it goes.
evidence: Card order by age: 40 minutes, 2 hours, 1 day, 3 days, 26 days. Beatriz's approve button is at y=1823 of a 1931px page. Every other card states its age precisely in the description line ("Registered 3 days ago", y=1156); the one deadline that carries a consequence is the only unquantified time on the screen.
direction: Order or hoist by time-to-sweep rather than by recency, so the card where inaction destroys data is the one you meet first, and put the remaining days in the banner as a number the way every other age on the page is stated.

where: the sidebar, x=0–223: nav ends at y≈222, the account chip sits at y≈870–905
finding: Nothing on this frame, or on the core team's home screen, tells anyone the queue exists. The route to /review is a link inside the closed account menu behind "Miriam Achebe", and neither the sidebar nor the chip carries a count, a dot, or a date. That is how a registration reaches 26 days old — card 5 in this very queue is the evidence that the entry point already failed once. Meanwhile 648px of the 900px sidebar column is empty, which is exactly where a standing count of waiting families and the soonest sweep date would cost nothing.
evidence: Sidebar holds four items (Check in, Insights, Events, Students) ending at y≈222; next ink is the account chip at y≈870. 648px, 72% of the column, is blank. The string "review" does not appear anywhere in the rendered dashboard prototype, so there is no pointer from the screen a core-team member actually opens on a Tuesday.
direction: Spend the empty sidebar: a persistent "Families to review — 5 waiting, 1 clears in 4 days" entry in the pointer-only column. The phone thumb bar is deliberately reserved for the four door tasks, so this should stay a desktop-side affordance rather than becoming a fifth tab.

where: the action pair at the foot of every card — Approve x=32–199, "Not ours" x=206–307, first instance at y=502–546
finding: Seven CSS pixels separate a button that writes irreversibly into Planning Center from a button that takes children off the roster and forgets the family's only phone number, and the guard is on the wrong one. A thumb aimed at the left edge of "Not ours" that lands 8px short hits "Approve and add", which fires immediately. The reverse mis-tap is caught, because "Not ours" arms a confirm. So the recoverable direction is protected and the permanent one is not, and the reviewer makes that 8px judgement five times, once per card, on a screen where every card looks the same.
evidence: Measured on the pixel row through y=524: brand fill #0ea5e9 runs x=32–199, card background resumes 199–206, the secondary fill #1e293b runs 206–307. Gap = 7px. Both buttons are exactly 44px tall (`min-h-11`) — the brief's marginal floor, not its comfortable one. Same geometry repeats at y=901, 1228, 1655, 2107.
direction: The two actions need real separation on touch — different rows, or the destructive one demoted out of the primary strip entirely — and the irreversible one needs at least the guard the recoverable one already has. The roster's "undo is never a dialog" rule does not govern this screen, so a confirm or a brief undo window is on the table here.

where: the amber merge link inside Elena Salgado's row (y=2069–2080, 26px above the Approve button at y=2107) and inside Ethan Nguyen's row (y=384–408)
finding: The control that exists to prevent the irreversible mistake is a 16px-tall target sitting 26px above the irreversible button. Reaching for "Somebody with this name is already on the roster" with a thumb and landing 20px low presses "Approve and add" — the exact outcome the link was there to prevent, reached by trying to prevent it. And at rest the link has no affordance at all: its only styling is `hover:underline`, which a touch screen never fires, so on a phone it is amber text on a card that already carries amber banner text of the same size, and the banner has a background this button does not.
evidence: `text-xs` is 12px with a 16px line box, and Tailwind preflight zeroes button padding and border, so the hit box is exactly 16px for Elena's one-line label and 32px for Ethan's two-line one — both under 44. Elena's ink runs y=2069–2080, Approve's top edge is y=2107. Beatriz's passive banner directly above (y≈1990) is the same `text-xs text-warn-400` on `bg-warn-500/10` with a ring. The child's name above it is also a 14px link to the student record with an ~18px box, so the row contains two invisible controls with completely different consequences and neither looks like a control.
direction: This has to become a real button on touch — chrome, padding, at least 44px, and clearly not the same object as the warn banners it currently imitates. It also has to stop being the nearest neighbour of the irreversible action; put separation between the merge decision and the approve decision, or resolve the merge before approve is offered at all.

where: the whole card stack in a 727px content window (top bar 0–48, tab bar 775–844), page 2348px
finding: One family fits per screen and there is no count, so a reviewer with three minutes on their phone spends all three on the two least urgent families in the queue and never learns the fifth one exists. Card 1 (registered 40 minutes ago) fills the window; card 5 — four days from the sweep that deletes the guardian's number — is 1990px down, past 2.7 screens of scrolling. Nothing above the fold says how many families are waiting or that one of them has a deadline, so the reviewer has no basis for deciding to skip ahead.
evidence: Content window is 727px (48–775). Card 1 spans y≈168–558, card 2 begins at y≈571 — one complete decidable family visible at a time. Page is 2348px, 3.2 viewport heights. Approve buttons at y=502, 901, 1228, 1655, 2107. The heading "Families to review" at y≈78 carries no number, and 102px of the fold above the first card is read-once explanatory prose.
direction: Put the size of the job and the presence of a deadline where the reviewer lands: a count in or beside the heading, and ordering that brings the expiring registration to the top rather than burying it under four that can wait. On a one-card-per-screen device the order of the queue is the entire triage mechanism.
